about: How the New Testament quotes, adapts or echoes the Old Testament. Written for this app in its own words; each row says whether the New Testament introduces the text as a citation, or only alludes to it, and (where we are confident) whether its wording follows the Hebrew or the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint). Scholars sometimes disagree about which wording lies behind a quotation. 'Differs' means the wording matches neither form closely.

entries.note: Matthew cites the Greek wording, which has 'virgin' (parthenos). The Hebrew word 'almah' means a young woman of marriageable age; the Greek translators chose 'virgin'.
A blend of Micah's Bethlehem oracle and God's word to David, 'you shall shepherd my people'. Matthew adjusts the wording to stress that Bethlehem is not least among the rulers of Judah.
Hosea speaks of Israel's exodus ('out of Egypt I called my son'). Matthew reads it as a pattern fulfilled in Jesus. The Hebrew has 'my son'; the Greek Old Testament reads 'his children'.
Rachel weeping for her children at Ramah; Jeremiah's lament over the exile is heard again at Bethlehem's slaughter.
No single Old Testament text says 'he shall be called a Nazarene'. Proposals include a wordplay on 'branch' (netzer, Isa 11:1), on 'Nazirite' (Judg 13:5), or a summary of the prophets' lowly Messiah.
All four Gospels apply Isaiah's 'voice in the wilderness' to John the Baptist. The Greek puts 'in the wilderness' with the voice; the Hebrew puts it with the road to be prepared.
Mark attributes a combined quotation to 'Isaiah the prophet'. The first part comes from Malachi and Exodus, the second from Isaiah.
The first of Jesus's three answers to the tempter in the wilderness, each from Deuteronomy, and each recalling Israel's forty years of testing.
The devil quotes Scripture too; Jesus answers by setting another text beside it.
Israel 'tested the Lord' at Massah (Exodus 17); Jesus refuses to repeat that test.
'You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him only', the first commandment's heart.
Matthew applies the light shining on 'Galilee of the nations' to the start of Jesus's public ministry.
The first of six 'you have heard... but I say to you' sayings in the Sermon on the Mount, each deepening a commandment.
On adultery, moving from the act to the intention of the heart.
On divorce; Jesus returns to 'the beginning' (Matthew 19:3-9).
The 'eye for an eye' rule limited retaliation in court; Jesus teaches non-retaliation in personal wrongs.
'You shall love your neighbour' is in the law; 'hate your enemy' is not, and is likely a common inference Jesus corrects.
Matthew's own rendering of the Hebrew, applied to Jesus's healings.
'I desire mercy, not sacrifice', quoted again in Matthew 12:7.
Jesus identifies John the Baptist as the messenger sent ahead; see also Mark 1:2 and Luke 7:27.
The first Servant Song, applied to Jesus's gentle healing ministry. Matthew's wording is closer to neither the Hebrew nor the standard Greek.
The sign of Jonah: three days and three nights in the belly of the fish, set beside the Son of Man in the heart of the earth.
The hardening verse of Isaiah's call, quoted in all four Gospels and Acts 28:26-27 to explain why many do not receive Jesus's word.
Mark's version is brief and troubling; commentators debate whether it describes purpose or result.
John joins Isaiah 6 and Isaiah 53 (verse 38) to explain unbelief.
The book of Acts ends with Paul quoting the same text to Jews in Rome.
Jesus's parables 'utter things hidden since the foundation of the world'.
Jesus uses the fourth commandment against a practice that dedicated goods to the Temple instead of supporting parents.
'This people honours me with their lips'; Matthew and Mark follow the Greek wording.
On marriage, Jesus goes back past Moses's concession to creation.
The king comes humble, on a donkey. John 12:15 gives a shorter form.
'Hosanna' ('save, we pray') and 'blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord', the pilgrim psalm of the feast.
Two prophets in one saying: the Temple as a house of prayer for all nations, and a robbers' den.
The Greek has 'you have prepared praise'; the Hebrew has 'you have established strength'.
The stone the builders rejected, taken up in Acts 4:11 and 1 Peter 2:7.
Jesus argues the resurrection from God's present-tense self-description: 'I am the God of Abraham'.
The Shema's command to love God, here with 'mind' where Deuteronomy has 'strength'.
Love of neighbour, the second commandment 'like' the first.
'The Lord said to my Lord': the most quoted Old Testament verse in the New Testament.
The 'abomination of desolation'; see also Mark 13:14.
'I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered', spoken on the night of the arrest.
Before the high priest Jesus joins two texts: the Son of Man coming on the clouds and being seated at God's right hand.
Matthew names Jeremiah but the thirty pieces of silver appear in Zechariah; Jeremiah supplies the potter and the field. Scholars explain it as a combined citation under the better-known prophet.
The cry from the cross opens Psalm 22, a prayer that moves from abandonment to praise. Mark 15:34 keeps the Aramaic.
The Shema as the first of all the commandments.
In the Nazareth synagogue Jesus reads a combined text, stopping before 'the day of vengeance', and says it is fulfilled today.
The widow of Zarephath and Naaman the Syrian: prophets sent to outsiders, which angers the hearers.
The presentation of the firstborn in the Temple.
John the Baptist in his own words.
'Zeal for your house will consume me', remembered by the disciples after the cleansing of the Temple.
'He gave them bread from heaven to eat', the text on which the Bread of Life discourse is built.
'They shall all be taught by God'.
'I said, you are gods', used in a short argument from the lesser to the greater.
The Palm Sunday acclamation.
'Fear not, daughter of Zion'; John's version is shorter than Matthew's.
'Lord, who has believed our report?'
'He who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me', applied to the betrayal.
'They hated me without a cause'.
'They divided my garments among them', which John links closely to the soldiers' dividing of the clothes.
'Not a bone of him shall be broken', which recalls both the Passover lamb and the righteous sufferer.
'They shall look on him whom they have pierced'; the Hebrew has 'on me', which John reads as God's own pierced one.
Peter uses two psalms of the betrayed righteous sufferer to justify choosing a replacement for Judas.
Peter explains Pentecost as the outpouring of the Spirit promised through Joel, adding 'in the last days'.
Peter reads David's confidence that God will not abandon his soul to the grave as speaking of the resurrection.
Peter's proof that David's lord is the risen Jesus.
The 'prophet like Moses'; quoted again by Stephen in Acts 7:37.
'In your seed all the families of the earth shall be blessed'.
The nations raging, applied to the opposition to Jesus in Jerusalem.
The Ethiopian official reads the Suffering Servant and Philip tells him the good news of Jesus.
'You are my Son, today I have begotten you' applied to the resurrection.
A light for the nations, claimed by Paul and Barnabas as their own mission.

James quotes the Greek form, 'that the rest of mankind may seek the Lord'. The Hebrew has 'that they may possess the remnant of Edom'. The two readings differ by a few letters, and the Greek reading supports Gentile inclusion.
'The righteous shall live by faith'. The Hebrew has 'his faith'; the Greek Old Testament has 'my faith'; Paul leaves the pronoun out.
God proved right in his words.
A chain of quotations on universal sinfulness, assembled from psalms and Isaiah.
'Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness', the centre of Paul's argument in Romans 4 and Galatians 3.
David's blessing on the one whose sin is covered.
'For your sake we are being killed all the day long'.
'Through Isaac shall your offspring be named'.
'Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated', a Semitic contrast of choice rather than an emotion.
'I will have mercy on whom I have mercy'.
'Not my people' called 'my people', applied to the Gentiles.
The stone of stumbling and the cornerstone are joined in one quotation, also found in 1 Peter 2:6-8.
'The one who does the commandments shall live by them', contrasted with the righteousness of faith.
Paul re-reads Moses's 'the word is near you' as the word of faith about Christ.
'Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved', with 'Lord' now read as Jesus.
'How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news'.
The voice of creation goes to all the earth.
Elijah and the seven thousand: a remnant chosen by grace.
'The Deliverer will come from Zion'. The Hebrew has 'to Zion'; Paul follows a form closer to the Greek.
'Vengeance is mine'.
'If your enemy is hungry, feed him'.
'The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me.'
The root of Jesse, in whom the Gentiles hope.
'I will destroy the wisdom of the wise'.
'Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.'
'What no eye has seen'. Paul's wording is looser than any known form of Isaiah.
'Who has known the mind of the Lord?'
'The two shall become one flesh', applied to sexual union.
'You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain', applied to supporting ministers.
The golden calf as a warning, in a chapter that reads the Exodus as a pattern for the Church.
'He has put all things in subjection under his feet.'
The first man Adam became a living being; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit.
'Death is swallowed up in victory'.
'O death, where is your sting?'
'I believed, and so I spoke.'
'Now is the acceptable time'.
'I will live in them and walk among them', the promise of God's dwelling applied to the Church.
'He has distributed freely, he has given to the poor.'
Abraham's faith as the pattern.
'In you shall all the nations be blessed.'
'Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the book of the law.'
'The righteous shall live by faith.'
'Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree', applied to the cross.
Paul presses the singular 'offspring' (seed) in the promises to Abraham.
'Rejoice, O barren one.'
'Cast out the slave and her son'; part of Paul's allegory of Hagar and Sarah.
The whole law fulfilled in one word: love your neighbour.
Paul writes 'he gave gifts', where the Hebrew has 'you received gifts'. The Aramaic Targum and the Syriac have the form Paul uses.
'Be angry and do not sin.'
Quoted for marriage, followed by 'this mystery is profound'.
The only commandment with a promise attached.
The opening chain of seven quotations proves the Son's superiority to angels.
'Let all God's angels worship him.' This line is not in the Hebrew text we have; it appears in the Greek Old Testament and in a Dead Sea Scrolls manuscript of Deuteronomy.
The royal wedding psalm applied to the Son.
The Lord who laid the foundation of the earth.
The seat at God's right hand.
Hebrews reads Psalm 8 of Jesus, and follows the Greek 'a little lower than the angels' where the Hebrew says 'than God (elohim)'.
The wilderness generation as a warning: 'Today, if you hear his voice'.
'A priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.'
The longest Old Testament quotation in the New Testament, on the new covenant.
'This is the blood of the covenant', echoed at the Last Supper.
'A body you have prepared for me.' The Hebrew has 'ears you have dug for me'; the Greek translators gave the sense differently.
The coming one will not delay; the righteous one lives by faith.
The Lord disciplines the one he loves.
'I will never leave you nor forsake you.'
The same verse Paul uses, read by James to show how faith is completed by action.
'God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.' Also quoted in 1 Peter 5:5.
'You shall be holy, for I am holy.'
'The word of the Lord remains forever.'
The cornerstone laid in Zion.
The rejected stone.
'A chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation': Israel's titles given to the Church.
'He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth.'
A long quotation on seeking peace.
'The dog returns to its own vomit.'
Jude quotes the book of Enoch (1 Enoch 1:9), which is not part of the Catholic canon. He cites it as a known prophecy, not as Scripture in the strict sense.
'Coming with the clouds' and 'every eye will see him, even those who pierced him' are joined.
The vision of one like a Son of Man draws on Daniel's Ancient of Days and the radiant man of Daniel 10.
The seraphim's 'Holy, holy, holy' sung around the throne.
The Lion of Judah and the Root of David.
God wipes away every tear and the Lamb shepherds the redeemed.
A new heaven and a new earth.
'The dwelling of God is with man', the covenant promise fulfilled.
The river of life and the tree of life, bringing Eden and Ezekiel's temple river together.
Mary's Magnificat echoes Hannah's song at the birth of Samuel, and draws on many psalms.
Zechariah's Benedictus is stitched from Old Testament phrases about redemption and the dawn.
The risen Jesus says the law, the prophets and the psalms speak of him.
The Son of Man at God's right hand.
The cry of dereliction in Aramaic.
The casting of lots for his clothes.
'Into your hands I commit my spirit.'
The works answering John's question are the signs promised by Isaiah.
The parable of the tenants rewrites Isaiah's song of the vineyard.
'I am the true vine' answers the picture of Israel as God's vine.
The Good Shepherd takes up God's promise to shepherd his flock himself.
'The Word became flesh and dwelt (tabernacled) among us' echoes the tent of meeting and the glory filling it.
The bronze serpent lifted up in the wilderness as a sign of the Son of Man lifted up.
'Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed.'
Paul reads the cloud, the sea, the manna and the rock as baptism and food for the people of God.
Enoch was taken up; the Greek says 'he pleased God', the Hebrew 'walked with God'.
The first Adam and the last Adam set side by side.
Every knee shall bow, here said of Jesus as Lord.
The Son as the image of the invisible God and the firstborn of creation echoes the creation of man in God's image and personified Wisdom.
The labourer deserves his wages, here joined with a saying of Jesus (Luke 10:7).
A people for his own possession.
